Silicon Benchmark Forecast Diagnostics

Team 16 — internal interpretation report

August 24, 2026

1 Executive summary

This report summarizes internal forecast behavior, not predictive accuracy. The benchmark outcomes remain unknown, so correlations and agreement can reveal stability or shared assumptions but cannot establish that a model is correct.

The present files contain 8 models and 2 prompt variants. Model-level values are aggregated before the models receive equal weight.

  • Coverage: 208 of 208 intervention–outcome cells.
  • Models represented: 8.
  • Fixed prompt variants represented: 2.
  • Median absolute candidate effect: 1.25% of the outcome scale.
  • Largest absolute candidate effect: 4.00% of the outcome scale.
  • Directional balance: 191 positive, 17 negative, and 0 exactly zero forecasts.
  • Median prompt-to-prompt range: 0.32% of the outcome scale; maximum: 25.00%.

3 Candidate consensus forecast map

This figure shows the primary provisional consensus from the three preselected family representatives. For every intervention and outcome, repeated completions are combined within prompts, prompts within models, and finally the 3 represented model families receive equal weight. Medians are used at every step to reduce the influence of an unusually extreme forecast.

What is an average treatment effect (ATE)?
An ATE is the predicted average outcome in the intervention group minus the predicted average in the control group. For example, this study includes an actual donation_ams outcome ranging from $0 to $10. An ATE of $1 would mean that participants receiving the intervention are forecast to donate one dollar more, on average, than participants reading a neutral control text. On the normalized heatmap that equals 10% of the donation scale. Similarly, a 5-point ATE on a 0–100 outcome equals 5% of its scale, while an ATE of 0.05 for the binary newsletter-signup outcome means a five-percentage-point difference. The sign matters: a negative ATE means the intervention group is forecast to score lower than the control group, which can be desirable for an outcome such as distrust.

Each tile expresses the consensus ATE as a fraction of that outcome’s possible range. The map is useful for seeing direction and relative magnitude across the complete intervention-by-outcome grid, spotting unexpectedly extreme cells, and checking whether substantive patterns are coherent. It does not show predictive accuracy because the human benchmark results remain hidden.

3.1 All-model diagnostic sensitivity map

This second map repeats the same hierarchical median rule using all 8 models with complete full-run results. Models are still combined within their developer families before the 3 families receive equal weight, so a family does not gain extra final weight merely because more variants were tested. This map is diagnostic only: it asks whether broadening the model roster materially changes the pattern of forecasts. Both maps use the same color scale, so their colors can be compared directly.

4 Outcome-level calibration

This figure asks whether the forecasting ensemble systematically assigns larger effects to some outcomes than others after accounting for their different native scales. Outcomes are sorted by the median absolute consensus effect, with the largest typical effects at the top.

All models with complete full-run results are included below. A model can look absent for a particular outcome when its median prompt gap is exactly zero: a zero-height bar is invisible. The statistic is the median, across interventions, of the absolute gap between the two fixed prompt variants for each outcome and model. It measures prompt sensitivity, not forecast magnitude or accuracy.

8 Interpretation checklist

Use this report to discuss the following questions with collaborators:

  1. Do the largest positive and negative forecasts make substantive sense given the interventions and outcome directions?
  2. Are any outcomes consistently assigned much larger effects than others after accounting for their native scales?
  3. Which cells are sensitive to prompt wording, and are those disagreements large enough to justify another fixed prompt variant?
  4. Once several models are present, do disagreements reflect magnitude, direction, or both?
  5. Are any routing failures, missing cells, or manual repairs present? If yes, do not lock a submission until they are resolved and documented.

8.1 What this report cannot establish

  • It cannot identify the most accurate model without human benchmark outcomes.
  • High prompt or model agreement does not imply calibration.
  • Low agreement does not identify which forecast is correct.
  • The report must not be used to remove a predeclared model merely because it disagrees with the others.
